model.description: Which model carries it. A shop declares fields on more than one thing and the two are not one namespace — `notes` on a product and `notes` on a customer are different fields, which is why the key is unique per model below rather than on its own.  It is a plain string and not an enum because the set is the app's models, which the seed already names; an enum here would be a second list to keep.

key.description: The shop's own name for it, as it appears in a segment and on a form. Lowercase and underscored because it is an identifier a person types into a query builder, and `@lower` means two shops cannot disagree with themselves about `VAT_Number` and `vat_number`.

defaultValue.description: What a form puts in the box before anybody types. Reaches the browser as the field rule's `default`, which is the same key a column's `@default` arrives under, so a generated form prefills a declared field the way it prefills a declared column and no screen applies it by hand.  A string whatever the type is: it is what somebody typed into a settings form, and the control coerces it the way it coerces anything else a person types. Storing a number here would need a second column nothing reads.

show.description: Whether a list offers it as a column. An affordance and never a rule — the value is readable by anyone who may read the row whatever this says, and a field hidden here is one screen's default rather than a permission (Invariant 6).

slot.description: Which pooled column carries it, or null when the pool for its type is full. Null is an ANSWER and not a failure: the field still stores and still displays, and only a segment naming it degrades to a scan. Refusing the declaration instead would tell a shop about an implementation detail they cannot see and cannot act on.  `@system` because the Data boundary allocates it — `@@extensible(max:)` fills it on create out of the pool that model declares, so no service here carries an allocator and nothing in this app names a slot. A caller choosing their own could take one another field already holds, and `@@unique([model, slot])` below is the second half of saying so.  A slot the payload STATES is honored rather than recomputed, which is what lets a restore put each field back where it was: re-deriving them would repoint live fields onto slots whose values were written for other keys.

notes.description: Staff-only. Field-level @allow is the tool for "some callers may read this column": the field is stripped from the response for anyone the policy rejects, without a line of service code saying so.  NOT @guarded — that is a system-context lock (@guarded / @guarded), not a level, and it takes no numeric argument. @guarded(5) does not parse.

userId.description: The credential behind this record, once there is one.  A `Customer` is the SHOP's record of a person — it exists the moment somebody checks out as a guest, with no password and no way back in. A `User` is the credential. They are two facts and the second is optional, which is why this is nullable and why it is here rather than the other way round: every buyer has a record, and only some of them have an account.  `@unique` because two accounts claiming one customer record is two people reading each other's orders. Written by the app — at checkout when the caller is signed in, and at registration when an address already has a history — never by the caller, which is what `@system` says.

fields.description: ─── What this shop decided a customer HAS ──────────────────────────────  Every shop on this deployment sells something different, so *what you record about a buyer* is the shop's question and not the framework's. One sells to businesses and wants a VAT number; one runs a loyalty scheme and wants a tier. Neither can be a column: a column is a migration, and a migration is a deploy, and `migrate.js` drops any column this file does not declare — so a shop that added its own would lose it on the next boot.  `fields` is what a person reads and edits. It is an ordinary blob, so it can hold anything and can be filtered on by nothing: litestone's query builder emits no `json_extract`, which is correct and is the whole problem — an audience nobody can select is a field nobody can use.

tools.name: discounts_aggregate
tools.description: Aggregates over Discount. The seed does not describe this method's argument.

code.description: What is typed. `@upper` so `welcome10` and `WELCOME10` are one code — a shopper reading a code off a poster is not going to match its case, and a lookup that fails on that is a support ticket.
code.title: Code

label.description: What the basket screen CALLS it. The code is an identifier; this is the sentence beside the amount, and a receipt saying `-$4.00 (WELCOME10)` tells a customer less than one saying `-$4.00 (10% off your first order)`.
label.title: Description

value.description: Percent: 0–100. Fixed: an amount in the shop's base currency. One column for two units, which is the cost of not having two tables — a FIELD validator here cannot see `kind`, so the bound that matters is declared at the model instead, below. `pricing.ts` still caps the discount at the subtotal, which is a different rule: this one is about what may be STORED, that one about what may be charged.  `@scale(2)` and not `@money`, and the two units are why: half the rows here are not money. What they share is the SCALE — a dollar's minor unit and a percentage's hundredth are both two places — so one exact integer column carries both without either reading being a rounded copy of itself. 1050 is $10.50 under `fixed` and 10.50% under `percent`, and the bound below is stated in the same units.
value.title: Value

minSubtotal.description: The floor this code is worth anything at. Zero means none. A whole number of USD minor units, not a decimal amount.
minSubtotal.title: Minimum spend

audience.description: WHO this code is for, in the shop's own vocabulary — `[{ key, op, value }]` over the fields it declared in `CustomField`. Null means everybody.  A blob rather than a relation because the terms are a document: the keys in them are rows in another table, so nothing in the schema could describe this shape without describing what that shop happens to have declared. It is the one place in this file where `Json` is the right answer rather than the absence of one.  It is read TWICE and by two different mechanisms, which is the whole point of it existing here: `customers.segment` compiles it to a `where` and asks SQLite who is in the audience, and `pricing.ts` compiles the same terms and asks `matchesQuery` whether ONE basket's customer is. One predicate, two readers — the shape `@frontierjs/toolbelt/match` exists for — because a list and a checkout answering differently is a code that a shopper can see advertised and cannot use.
audience.title: Audience

startsAt.description: The window. Both nullable — a code with no start is live now, a code with no end runs until somebody turns it off.
startsAt.title: Starts

maxRedemptions.description: How many times it may be used, and how many times it has been. Null means no limit.  `redemptions` is `@system`: the application writes it, never a caller, and never a merchant editing the form — a counter a person can set is not a count of anything. It is incremented inside `carts.checkout`'s transaction by read-modify-write rather than `{ increment: 1 }`, for `stock`'s reason: an atomic operator computes the new value inside SQLite where no validator can see it, so the limit would be passed and the constraint would never fire (`FJS-D27`). The transaction is what makes the read-then-write safe, and it is the same transaction the order is written in — a code redeemed by an order that rolls back was not redeemed.
maxRedemptions.title: Redemption limit

inputSchema.title: Discount
inputSchema.description: A code somebody types at the till.  ─── Why a shopper may not read this table ────────────────────────────────  `@@gate("5.5.5.5")` — staff only, read included. Every other thing a shopper interacts with here is readable at 0, because a storefront has to list it; a discount code is the exception, and the reason is that listing them IS the exploit. `GET /api/discounts` answering the table hands every unreleased code to anyone who asks, and a shop's codes are worth money.  So the shopper never reads a row: they send a string to `carts.applyDiscount`, which validates it through the SYSTEM client and answers the basket with the money recalculated — the same shape `StockReservation` uses for holds, and for the same reason. What comes back is what this code is worth to THIS basket, which is the only fact about it they are entitled to.

description.description: Optional on a draft, mandatory the moment it goes on sale.  `site/` bakes one HTML file per ACTIVE product and takes that page's meta description from this column, and `@@fts` searches it for words that are on no page — so an active product with no description is a storefront page that is unfindable and unreadable by a crawler, and nothing anywhere fails. The two columns are individually fine and the PAIR is the rule, which until `@required(where: …)` meant it had to be written twice: once in whatever service handler ran first, once in the form.  `where:` reads this row's own columns and nothing else, which is what buys the `CHECK` in the DDL — so it holds against a seed, a migration, `asSystem()` and a raw INSERT, not only against a request. It reaches the browser as `x-litestone-required-where`, so ticking Active on the product form makes this box required with nothing reloaded.  One asymmetry worth knowing: the CHECK is `IS NOT NULL`, so an empty string satisfies the boundary while the browser's own `required` refuses it. The form is the stricter of the two here, in the direction that costs a keystroke rather than a refused write.

In a stockroom the sheet is made on the same phone, in the same minute, with no signal — so at the moment the first count is written there IS no server id, because nothing has been inserted anywhere. `@default(uuid())` puts the key in the browser's hands: `x-mint` crosses with the schema, sierra states the key on the create, and the count that follows references a sheet the server has never heard of and is still correct when both writes drain.  `InventoryMovement` keeps `Int @id` and is right to: nothing references a movement, so nobody ever needs its key before the server has one. cancelAtPeriodEnd.description: Asked to stop — at the boundary, rather than now.  A flag beside `active` and not a fifth status, and the choice is the substance. A `cancelling` state would be declared, so the console's button set would stay derived from `@@transitions`; it would also double what every reader has to grade. The renewal, `unpaidInvoices`, the dunning read and both row policies above ask ONE question about `status`, and *is this live* becoming a set membership is the shape that goes wrong in one caller and nowhere else.  So *live* stays one comparison and this decides only what a renewal does when the period closes. The cost is recorded rather than argued away: it is invisible to `@@transitions`, so Stop renewing and Resume are the first buttons in this app that cannot be derived from what the schema declares.  `@system`, because it is set through `subscriptions.cancel` and `subscriptions.resume` — which keep the gate and the row policies — and never by a caller naming the column on a patch.
